nameStory: The rusty blackbird gets its name from the rusty-brown edges on its feathers that appear especially prominent during fall and winter months. This rusty coloring is most noticeable when the birds aren't in their sleek breeding plumage, giving them a weathered, oxidized appearance that sets them apart from other blackbirds.
description: The rusty blackbird is a medium-sized songbird that's part of the blackbird and oriole family. Males in breeding season are glossy black with a slight greenish sheen, while females are more grayish-brown. During fall and winter, both sexes develop distinctive rusty-brown feather edges that give the bird its name. They're slightly smaller than grackles but larger than red-winged blackbirds, with a straight, pointed bill perfect for foraging.

idTips.label: Rusty feather edges
idTips.description: In fall and winter, look for brownish-rust colored edges on the wing and body feathers that create a scaly or mottled appearance, especially noticeable in good light

idTips.label: Yellow eyes
idTips.description: Bright pale yellow eyes that stand out against the dark head - much more yellow than the dark eyes of red-winged blackbirds

idTips.label: Straight, pointed bill
idTips.description: Thin, sharp-pointed bill that's noticeably straighter and more needle-like than the slightly curved bills of grackles

idTips.label: Wet habitat preference
idTips.description: Almost always found near water - swampy areas, wet woodlands, or boggy spots where they wade and probe for food

idTips.label: Creaky call
idTips.description: Makes a harsh, rusty-hinge sound like 'ksh-leep' or metallic creaking noises rather than the clear notes of other blackbirds

habitat: Rusty blackbirds prefer wet, forested areas and are almost always found near water in New England. Look for them in swampy woodlands, beaver ponds, boggy areas, and wetlands surrounded by trees. They're particularly drawn to places where they can wade in shallow water while staying close to forest cover.

seasonality.spring: During spring migration in March and April, rusty blackbirds pass through New England in small flocks, still showing some rusty feather edges from winter that gradually molt away.
seasonality.summer: Very rare in summer as most head north to Canada to breed. Any summer sightings would be exceptional and worth reporting to birding organizations.
seasonality.fall: Fall migration from September through November brings the best viewing opportunities as flocks return south, with rusty feather edges beginning to develop on fresh plumage.
seasonality.winter: Some individuals winter in southern New England, showing full rusty plumage and often joining mixed blackbird flocks at feeders and in agricultural areas.

funFact: Rusty blackbirds have experienced one of the most catastrophic population crashes of any North American bird, declining by an estimated 85-95% since the 1960s, making them rarer than many species we consider endangered - yet scientists still aren't sure exactly why they're disappearing so rapidly.
confusionNotes: Most often confused with Brewer's blackbirds (which are rare in New England) and female red-winged blackbirds. Remember: rusty blackbirds have yellow eyes and rusty feather edges in fall/winter, while red-winged blackbirds have dark eyes and lack the rusty coloring. Rusty blackbirds also prefer wetter habitats than Brewer's blackbirds.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called a 'blackbird,' rusty blackbirds are actually more closely related to grackles and were once called 'rusty grackles.' They're part of the New World blackbird family, which is completely unrelated to the European blackbirds that inspired the Beatles song.
compareHints: Rusty blackbirds can be distinguished from their close relative, Brewer's blackbird, by their preference for wet, forested habitats rather than open areas, and by their yellow eyes (Brewer's have dark eyes). In New England, Brewer's blackbirds are quite rare, making rusty blackbird the more likely species you'll encounter near wetlands, though both share similar rusty winter plumage.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its close relative the Rusty Blackbird, Brewer's males are more iridescent black (versus rusty-brown edges), and both species have yellow eyes, but Rusty Blackbirds are much more common in New England wetlands.
